messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 74
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Pharmacist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body, Avoid Feelings: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Rosa's Story

Rosa Hernández is a seventy-four-year-old widow—though not by the death of her first husband, but by her own deliberate distance from him after nearly forty years of marriage. She had worked as a pharmacist for fifty-two years, a career that gave her identity, competence, and the quiet authority that came from helping people navigate their medications and their fears. She had been good at it: meticulous, calm, trusted by her community. But that woman feels like someone else now.

The violence began when Rosa was in her late sixties. Her husband, a man she had believed she knew, began to drink more heavily after his retirement. One evening, after she had questioned him about a late night out, he grabbed her by the arm—not gently—and forced her against the kitchen counter. His hands were around her throat. She remembered the pressure, the shock that this could happen in her own home, the way her vision tunneled. When he finally released her, she was on the floor, gasping. He apologized the next morning. She told herself it was an isolated incident, a moment of stress, something that happened to other women, not to her. But it happened again. And again. Each time he was remorseful; each time she found reasons to stay, to believe it would change. By the time she finally left, she had internalized a story about herself that felt immutable: she was weak, foolish, a woman who had failed to see what was in front of her. She had lost faith in her own judgment, in people, in the idea that the world was a place where she could be safe.

Now, three years into her separation and living alone in a small house in a quiet suburb, Rosa is trapped by the architecture of her own vigilance. When someone at the grocery store mentions family—a casual remark about a daughter's visit or a grandchild—Rosa's chest tightens. These comments thrust her back into the kitchen, into the moment when she realized her own home had become a cage. The mention of family, of closeness, of the bonds she once believed in, carries the full weight of that betrayal. Her body responds before her mind can catch up: her shoulders hunch, her jaw clenches, and she finds herself scanning the room for exits. The trigger is not the words themselves but what they represent—the illusion of safety, the lie that love protects you.

Similarly, when someone tries to get emotionally close to her—a neighbor who wants to sit with her on the porch, a daughter-in-law who reaches for her hand—Rosa feels a surge of panic that she cannot fully explain. The closeness itself becomes dangerous. She pulls away, makes excuses. She has come to believe that allowing anyone near her emotionally is a form of surrender, another way of being weak and foolish. And the sound of a door opening or slamming—any door in her house, even the gentle click of the refrigerator—sends her entire body into a state of readiness. She is listening, always listening, for the moment when someone might enter. The trigger floods her with the physical sensation of being trapped, of not knowing what is coming.

These triggers do not arrive in isolation. When Rosa hears a door, when someone mentions family, when emotional closeness is offered, her body floods with alarm. Her muscles tense; she feels constantly ready to react to danger, as though a threat is always imminent. She monitors every sound in her home, listening for the particular creak of footsteps, the particular timbre of an intrusion. Even inside her own house, behind locked doors, she feels on guard. This hypervigilance is exhausting, but it feels necessary—it feels like the price of survival.

And with the threat comes the memory. When her body is activated, when she is tense and listening, the images return. She sees the kitchen in snapshots—the counter, his face, her own hands braced against the wall. Her body remembers the position she was in, the way her spine curved, the angle of her neck. These are not coherent narratives but fragments, each one a still photograph that burns itself into her awareness. When the memories surface, shame floods through her, a shame so intense that she has come to believe it is the truest thing about her. She is ashamed of what happened, ashamed that she stayed, ashamed that she did not see it coming. The shame reinforces her conviction that she is weak, that she failed, that she is no longer the capable woman she once was.

To manage the unbearable weight of these memories and the shame they carry, Rosa has begun to avoid her own body. She does not look in the mirror. She wears loose clothing and does not think about the physical form that once felt like home. She avoids feeling anything strongly—she has learned to dampen her emotions, to move through the world in a kind of protective numbness. She avoids other people. She retired from the pharmacy two years ago, citing fatigue, though the truth was more complicated. Being around people triggered the hypervigilance; it made her feel exposed. Without the structure of work, without the professional identity that had sustained her, she has become increasingly isolated. Her daughter calls less frequently now; Rosa's withdrawal has been consistent enough that her family has learned to give her space. She tells herself this is what she wants, what she needs, but the isolation has deepened her sense that she is incapable of the connections that once defined her life.

The avoidance works, in a way. When she is alone, when she does not allow herself to feel, when she does not engage with people or her own body, the immediate distress diminishes. But the cost is accumulating. She has lost her work identity, her social connections, and increasingly, her sense of who she is. The avoidance has become its own kind of prison, and it feeds back into her conviction that she is no longer capable, that she is fundamentally weak, that people cannot be trusted. The more she avoids, the more real these beliefs become. The more real these beliefs become, the more triggers proliferate—now even the thought of a family gathering sends her into a spiral of dread.

It was her daughter who finally insisted she see someone. Rosa came to the appointment reluctant, convinced that nothing could help, that she was broken beyond repair. What she hopes for, though she hardly dares to name it, is a way back to herself—not to who she was before, but to someone who can exist in the world without constant fear, who can look at her own reflection without shame, who can sit with her grandchildren without the walls closing in. But first, she will have to face the very things she has spent three years learning to avoid.
